To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the equilibrium Oosawa model is readily generalized to include arbitrarily large deviations from ideality and that these deviations are expected to affect the solubility of a protein and the breadth of its polymer size distribution in a manner that is proportional to the fractional (logaritmic) change in its thermodynamic activity.

the thermodynamic activity and the equilibrium solubilities of self-associating proteins are both reduced by the presence of volume-excluding crowding species, while the breadth of the equilibrium polymer size distribution is broadened.

(i) the equilibrium Oosawa model for rod-like fibers can be recast into a form that is readily extended to account for the effects of volume occupancy by an arbitrary inert species and (ii) volume occupancy by an arbitrarily large inert species can have significant effects on the equilibrium solvation and on the equilibrium distribution of protein fiber size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of volume exclusion on the kinetics and thermodynamics of protein self-association and fiber assembly.
the effects of volume-excluding macmolecules on the assembly of rod-like proteins.
understanding how the presence of inert volume-excluded macromolecules (such as proteins, DNA, or polysaccharides) affects the equilibrium distribution of self-associating species in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of inert volume-exclusion macromolecules upon the equilibrium properties of protein fiber formation are qualitatively similar to those of the excluded-volume effect.
volume exclusion effects are expected to be small, but not negligible, and that their effect on the distribution of polymer size is expected to be greater than that on the solubility of monomer.

, in the presence of volume-excluding macroparticles, the equilibrium distribution of oligomers of a protein that self-assembles into fibers is determined by the relative size of the macroparticle to that of the protein monomer and the relative thermodynamic activity of the monomer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

volume-excluding macroparticles, whether they are inert or self-associating, have the potential to affect the equilibrium solubilities of proteins and the equilibrium distributions of their polymer size.

the effect of volume exclusion on equilibrium properties is qualitatively the same as the effect of a change in thermodynamic activity, and that the magnitude of the effect is proportional to the fractional change in the activity of monomer (i.e., the change in activity is additive with respect to volume exclusion).

the equilibrium solubilities and polymer size distributions of self-associating proteins can be strongly influenced by the presence of inert volume-exclusion macromolecules, even when the latter are present only at low concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, at equilibrium, the effects of crowding on protein fiber formation are essentially the same as those on protein solubility.

volume-exclusion effects can have a significant effect on both solubility (i.e., the concentration of monomer at which polymerization occurs) and upon the breadth of the equilibrium polymer size distribution.
the effect of volume occupancy by inert molecules on equilibrium protein polymerization can be readily calculated using a simple scaling relationship.
